title: IISS Shangri-La Dialogue 2026 | United States’ Strategy for Peace in the Indo-Pacific
channel: The International Institute for Strategic Studies
summary: The US defence secretary at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue sets out deterrence by denial against China's build-up, allied burden sharing and warmer US-China ties after a Trump-Xi summit.

assertions.quote: there is rightful alarm regarding China's historic military buildup and the expansion of its military activities in the region and beyond.
We will build and sustain a strong denial defense in the Western Pacific that ensures aggression is infeasible, escalation unattractive, and war deemed irrational.

verdicts.note: Deterrence by denial is the mainstream strategy and has held so far, but whether it would deter China in a crisis is untested and depends on capabilities still being built.

assertions.quote: Under President Trump's leadership, relations between the United States and China are better than they've been in many years.

verdicts.note: A 2026 Trump-Xi summit eased the trade war and agreed a strategic-stability framing, but military competition, export controls and Taiwan tensions remain.
The Department of War's December 2025 preface says US-China relations are 'stronger than they have been in many years' under Trump, an official self-assessment rather than a measure.
US intelligence points to US-China cooperation under the Busan Agreement amid continuing rivalry, which shows some improvement but does not establish relations at a multi-year high.

assertions.quote: By maintaining open lines of military-to-military communication, we can coordinate, deconflict, and reduce the risk of miscalculation.

verdicts.note: Hotlines and incident agreements lower the odds that an accident escalates, though China has often cut these channels during crises.

FRI's median expert thought a crisis communications network among nuclear states would cut the risk of nuclear catastrophe by 25% (superforecasters 15%): support for the mechanism, but for nuclear catastrophe in general rather than a US-China war.

DoD keeps lines open 'to reduce risk and manage crisis', but notes China uses military engagements as a tool to punish or reward, cancelling them when tensions rise, which limits their value in a crisis.

The case file credits Cold War reconnaissance that reduced dangerous misunderstandings, and the arms-control and summit cooperation from SALT to Reagan-Gorbachev, with lowering the risk of a nuclear accident and building trust. This is a US-Soviet analogy, not evidence on US-China military channels.

CNAS credits the 1972 Incidents at Sea Agreement with reducing US-Soviet escalation risk, but notes the US and China signed the 1998 and 2014 air and maritime agreements and incidents continued, so channels help only partly.

Both governments welcomed the resumption of high-level military-to-military channels, and the US side said open communication keeps competition from veering into conflict; an official view, not evidence of the effect.

assertions.quote: President Lee's decision to increase defense spending to the new global standard of 3.5%

verdicts.note: South Korea, Japan, the Philippines and Australia have all announced defence budget increases in 2025 and 2026.
In 2025 Japan's spending rose 9.7 percent to its highest burden since 1958, Taiwan's rose 14 percent (largest since at least 1988, with a 5 percent of GDP goal by 2030) and South Korea's 2.6 percent.
The Munich Security Report says many Indo-Pacific players have stepped up their own defence efforts in response to Chinese coercion and doubts about US guarantees.

assertions.quote: We're focused on that. We can do two things at one time.
